Fit joinpoint regression models

Source: R/joinpoint.R
joinpoint.Rd

Fits joinpoint (segmented line) regression models to one or more trend series (Kim et al. 2000). For each cohort (combination of by values) the best fitting model with kmin to kmax joinpoints is found by an exhaustive grid search, the number of joinpoints is selected with the chosen criterion, and the annual percent change (APC), average annual percent change (AAPC) and joinpoint locations are estimated with confidence intervals.

Usage

joinpoint(
  data,
  x,
  y = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  se = NULL,
  count = NULL,
  population = NULL,
  type = c("rate", "crude_rate", "proportion", "percent", "count", "other"),
  rate_per = 1e+05,
  family = c("gaussian", "poisson", "binomial"),
  log = TRUE,
  variance = NULL,
  autocorrelation = 0,
  vcov = NULL,
  kmin = 0,
  kmax = NULL,
  method = c("wbic", "bic", "bic3", "mbic", "dds", "permutation", "lrt"),
  ci_method = NULL,
  covariates = NULL,
  continuous = FALSE,
  overdispersion = FALSE,
  exclude = NULL,
  shift = 0,
  jump = NULL,
  comparability_ratio = NULL,
  cr_variance = 0,
  interval = "Annual",
  control = jp_control()
)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

x

Independent variable (column name, bare or quoted), usually the calendar year. Values must be unique within each cohort.

y

Dependent variable (a rate, proportion, count or other value). May be omitted when count and population are given.

by

Optional character vector of by-variables defining cohorts.

se

Optional column of standard errors of y (on the original scale).

count, population

Optional columns of counts and populations (or numerators and denominators) used to calculate crude rates, proportions or percents and their standard errors.

type

Type of dependent variable: "rate" (a provided crude or age adjusted rate), "crude_rate", "proportion", "percent", "count" or "other".

rate_per

Rate multiplier for calculated crude rates.

family

"gaussian" (default) fits by (weighted or generalized) least squares. "poisson" fits a Poisson regression of count with log link and population as exposure, and "binomial" a logistic regression of count events out of population trials, both by maximum likelihood (Czajkowski et al. 2008); for these the segment changes are percent changes in the rate or in the odds.

log

Fit the log-linear model ln(y) = xb (TRUE, default) or the linear model y = xb (FALSE).

variance

Heteroscedastic errors option: "constant", "se" (standard errors provided or calculated) or "poisson". Defaults to "se" when standard errors are available and "constant" otherwise.

autocorrelation

First order autocorrelation of the errors: a number in (-1, 1), or "estimate" to estimate it from the data.

vcov

Optional variance-covariance matrix of the responses (single cohort only).

kmin, kmax

Minimum and maximum number of joinpoints. kmax = NULL uses the recommended maximum for the number of observations.

method

Model selection method: "wbic" (weighted BIC, default), "bic", "bic3", "mbic" (modified BIC), "dds" (data dependent selection) or "permutation" for least squares fits; "wbic", "bic", "bic3" or "lrt" (sequential Monte Carlo likelihood ratio test) for Poisson and binomial fits.

ci_method

Confidence interval method for APCs, AAPCs and joinpoint locations: "empirical" (empirical quantile, the default for least squares fits with grid joinpoints) or "parametric" (the only method for Poisson and binomial fits and for continuous joinpoints). Parametric intervals condition on the estimated joinpoints, except the interval of a joinpoint location; for Poisson and binomial fits they are Wald intervals and the joinpoint interval is based on the profile deviance.

covariates

Optional one-sided formula of covariates adjusted for in every segment, for example ~ factor(month) for seasonality. The covariates are centered, so the fitted trend refers to their average. Their names must differ from those of the model's own coefficients: intercept, slope, jump and delta1, delta2, and so on.

continuous

Estimate joinpoints anywhere between observations (Hudson 1966) instead of only at the grid points: every placement of joinpoints at observations or inside the gaps between them is examined, so the least squares solution is exact. Placements are those allowed by the placement rules and their limits, in which an observation on a joinpoint counts toward one of its two segments. The limits of the parametric joinpoint intervals are located inside the gaps. Available for least squares fits with parametric intervals and selection by a criterion; n_grid is not used.

overdispersion

For Poisson and binomial fits, estimate a dispersion parameter (quasi-likelihood) instead of fixing it at 1 (maximum likelihood): the Pearson statistic of the largest model divided by the number of observations less its coefficients and joinpoints, and at least 1. It scales the Wald covariances and the deviances in the criteria and is reported by model_selection().

exclude

Values of x to exclude from model fitting. Excluded points are kept in the data and graphs.

shift

Constant added to x before fitting.

jump

For coding changes: the last value of x under the old coding. Fits the jump model, or the comparability ratio model when comparability_ratio is given.

comparability_ratio, cr_variance

Comparability ratio (new coding over old coding) and its variance for the comparability ratio model.

interval

Interval label of x used in output, e.g. "Annual" or "Monthly".

control

Settings from jp_control().

Value

An object of class joinpoint.

References

Kim HJ, Fay MP, Feuer EJ, Midthune DN (2000). Permutation tests for joinpoint regression with applications to cancer rates. Statistics in Medicine 19:335-351.

Clegg LX, Hankey BF, Tiwari R, Feuer EJ, Edwards BK (2009). Estimating average annual percent change in trend analysis. Statistics in Medicine 28:3670-3682.

Kim HJ, Luo J, Chen HS, et al. (2017). Improved confidence interval for average annual percent change in trend analysis. Statistics in Medicine 36:3059-3074.

Kim HJ, Chen HS, Midthune D, et al. (2023). Data-driven choice of a model selection method in joinpoint regression. Journal of Applied Statistics 50:1992-2013.

Hudson DJ (1966). Fitting segmented curves whose join points have to be estimated. Journal of the American Statistical Association 61:1097-1129.

Czajkowski M, Gill R, Rempala G (2008). Model selection in logistic joinpoint regression with applications to analyzing cohort mortality patterns. Statistics in Medicine 27:1508-1526.

Examples

tb <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Tuberculosis")
fit <- joinpoint(tb, x = year, y = rate, kmax = 3, ci_method = "parametric")
fit
#> Joinpoint regression (log-linear model, constant variance)
#> Model selection: WBIC; confidence intervals: parametric
#> 
#> Cohort: All
#>   Joinpoints: 3 (1947, 1954, 1981)
#>   1900-1947  APC = -3.720*  [-3.911, -3.528]
#>   1947-1954  APC = -14.660*  [-18.349, -10.803]
#>   1954-1981  APC = -8.967*  [-9.407, -8.526]
#>   1981-1998  APC = -4.520*  [-5.390, -3.642]
#>   AAPC Full Range (1900-1998) = -6.144*  [-6.504, -5.783]
#> 
#> * Significantly different from zero at alpha = 0.05.
apc(fit)
#>   model final  ci_method segment start  end   estimate      lower      upper
#> 1     3  TRUE parametric       1  1900 1947  -3.719816  -3.911050  -3.528200
#> 2     3  TRUE parametric       2  1947 1954 -14.659682 -18.349395 -10.803234
#> 3     3  TRUE parametric       3  1954 1981  -8.967482  -9.406536  -8.526299
#> 4     3  TRUE parametric       4  1981 1998  -4.520365  -5.390354  -3.642375
#>    statistic      p_value significant
#> 1 -37.890172 2.826091e-56        TRUE
#> 2  -7.127769 2.692260e-10        TRUE
#> 3 -38.619106 5.804778e-57        TRUE
#> 4 -10.042718 2.937842e-16        TRUE
